world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Fesl, Eve. 1985. Ganai: a study of the Aboriginal languages of Gippsland. MA thesis, Monash University; not accessible online

new_statements.quote: Normally e was an open front vowel slightly below cardinal [ɛ], but when followed by a nasal, whether under the main accent or not, was a much closer vowel and approached a position below cardinal [e]. [...] When a was long and accented it had a low back vowel [ɑ] as allophone, while in an unaccented position it was pronounced like the [ʌ] of Wembawemba. Before a final n or ŋ however, it remained a front [a], whether it was accented or not. The rules governing vowel length differed from those current in the Kulin languages: long vowels were rare; the only ones noted were u in ŋu [ˈŋuː] belt, and accented a before final ɖ, dj and ɳ.
new_statements.citation: Hercus, Luise A. 1986. Victorian Languages: A Late Survey. Pacific Linguistics B-77. Canberra: Australian National University. (= Hercus 1969, The Languages of Victoria: A Late Survey, AIAS, p. 189.)
new_statements.locator: Sec. 6.4 'Gippsland: the Ganai language', p. 165 (PDF p. 195); stress-marked forms in sec. 6.4 pp. 164-165 and sec. 7.8 'Gippsland vocabulary' pp. 240-242 (PDF pp. 270-272)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (334 pp., text layer; PDF page = printed page + 30). Printed p. 165 (PDF p. 195), sec. 6.4 'Gippsland: the Ganai language', contains the quoted passage word for word; the reader's '[...]' correctly elides one sentence ('The close pronunciation was also noted before ɳ in breɳ [ˈbreɳ] hand.'). I read all of sec. 6.4 (pp. 163-165): it names the five Ganai tribes (Bratauolung, Brabralung, Braiakaulung, Krauatungalung, Tatungalung = 'Kurnai' of Fison & Howitt), data from Lake Tyers, chiefly Brabralung via Mrs Connolly's son, so the languoid is gana1278 (Ganai/Kurnai, ISO unn), not a neighbour. Nowhere in 6.4 does Hercus state where the main accent falls; the only accent content is the vow…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No source states a placement rule. Hercus's phonetic notes establish that Ganai had a word-level stress accent ('main accent', accented vs unaccented vowels), and every Ganai word she transcribed from her Lake Tyers consultants carries the tonic-stress mark on the first syllable ([ˈbUlen,djetI] stomach, [ˈbandje,won] boots, [ˈbUndI] waddy, [ˈgana i] man, [ˈmIrI,gan] dog, [ˈyalAman] several, [ˈwendolo] how?, [ˈbraˑˌgalAg,ran] boy). The provisional reading 'fixed-initial' is inferred from these consistently marked transcriptions plus her explicit first-syllable rules for the neighbouring Victorian languages in the same book, not from a stated rule for Ganai.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not stated for Ganai; the transcriptions show a secondary stress (marked) on the second or third syllable of some polysyllables, e.g. [ˈbUlen,djetI], [ˈbandje,won], [ˈbIndjU,laŋ], [ˈbU,ɖaˑlak], [ˈmIrI,gan]; the compound bra-galagran carries two tonic marks.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Hercus notes the data are 'inevitably meagre' (one main speaker, Mrs Connolly's son, Brabralung dialect with some Bratauolung items).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms elicited from remembered vocabulary in the 1960s; no phrase-level stress information. Vowel length is stated to be conditioned (partly by accent) and non-phonemic.
new_statements.identity_note: Hercus's Ganai data come from Lake Tyers, chiefly the Brabralung dialect (used as the mission lingua franca) with some Bratauolung (Yarram) items, all within gana1278. Mathews 1907 describes 'Birdhawal' (Bidawal/Muk-thang, far East Gippsland), which he treats as the same Gippsland language and Wikipedia lists as a Gunai dialect; Glottolog has no separate Bidhawal languoid (search returned nothing). Fesl 1985 covers all five Ganai tribal dialects from 19th-century records plus Hercus's tapes; her ch. 6 'Narigu' (Ngarigu, Monaro) is a different (Yuin) language.

sources.note: No explicit rule of stress placement for Ganai. The phonetic notes (p. 165) speak of vowels 'under the main accent', 'accented' vs 'unaccented' positions and 'accented a' before final retroflex/palatal consonants, i.e. a word-level stress accent exists. Every Ganai form in 6.4 and in the Gippsland vocabulary (pp. 240-242) carries the tonic-stress mark on the first syllable (e.g. [ˈbUlen,djetI] stomach, [ˈbandje,won] boots, [ˈgIran] rump, [ˈgana i] man, [ˈmIrI,gan] dog, [ˈyalAman] several, [ˈwendolo] how), with a secondary stress on a later syllable in some trisyllables. sources.citation: Mathews, R. H. 1907. Language of the Birdhawal tribe, in Gippsland, Victoria. Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society 46(186): 346-359.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: open copy online (also: harvard online access (harvardkey))
sources.note: 'Orthography' section (pp. 347-349) gives letter values only; the only accent remark (p. 349) is that the monosyllable wruk 'ground' 'can be got exactly by making it wu-ruk', and then pronouncing it as one syllable, with the accent on the last letter' — a pronunciation aid for initial wr-/mr- clusters, not a stress rule. Birdhawal is described as the Gippsland language ('the language prevailing over the whole area is the Birdhawal, or dialects of the Birdhawal').

sources.citation: Fesl, Eve. 1985. Ganai: A study of the Aboriginal languages of Gippsland based on 19th century materials. MA thesis, Monash University. viii+373 pp. Ch. 8 Phonology pp. 80-92.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: No statement of stress placement of her own; the only mention of accent is on p. 90 (PDF p. 107) where she quotes Hercus 1969: 189 verbatim on accented/unaccented vowel allophones. Her phonemicised forms and word lists are not stress-marked. Ch. 9.1 notes that just over 41% of Ganai nouns are monosyllabic, most of the rest disyllabic.
